summary.en: Mandarin has four tones plus a neutral tone. The same syllable with a different tone is a different word: mā 妈, má 麻, mǎ 马, mà 骂.

en: First tone (ā) is high and flat. Second tone (á) rises, like asking "huh?". Third tone (ǎ) dips low. Fourth tone (à) falls sharply, like a firm "no!".
Tone marks sit on the main vowel: a or e first, the o in ou, otherwise the last vowel.
In the drills, look at the character and pick the pinyin with the right tone. If your browser has a Chinese voice, tap the speaker to hear it.

summary.en: Some syllables lose their tone and are said short and light: bàba 爸爸, xièxie 谢谢, 吗 ma.

en: Neutral syllables have no tone mark in pinyin.
Doubled family words (妈妈, 哥哥), particles (吗, 呢, 了, 的) and suffixes like 子 in 桌子 are usually neutral.
Pick the spelling that shows which syllable is neutral.

summary.en: Most words have two syllables, so tones are learned best in pairs: 中国 Zhōngguó (1+2), 老师 lǎoshī (3+1).

en: There are 20 possible combinations of four tones plus neutral. Learning words as pairs trains your ear faster than single syllables.
In each drill, pick the correct tone pattern for the whole word.

title.en: Tone changes: 3rd tone, 不 and 一

summary.en: Two third tones in a row: the first becomes second (你好 sounds like ní hǎo). 不 becomes bú and 一 becomes yí before a fourth tone.

en: Dictionaries write the original tone. Speakers change it in these cases, and HSK materials often show the spoken tone for 不 and 一.
不 bù becomes bú before a fourth tone: 不是 bú shì.
一 yī becomes yí before a fourth tone (一个 yí gè) and yì before other tones (一天 yì tiān).
In the drills, pick the pinyin as it is actually said.

summary.en: Characters are written in a fixed stroke order: top to bottom, left to right, horizontal before vertical.

en: The basic rules: top before bottom, left before right, horizontal before vertical, outside before inside, and close a box last.
Correct order makes characters easier to remember and to read in handwriting.
In the drills, trace each character stroke by stroke. The engine checks the order and direction.

summary.en: 了 after a verb marks it as done (我吃了 "I ate"). 了 at the end can mark a new situation (下雨了 "it is raining now").

en: 了 is not a past tense. It shows that an action is completed, or that something has changed.
Verb + 了 + object: 我买了一本书 "I bought a book".
At the end of a sentence 了 announces a change: 我饿了 "I am hungry now". Negated actions use 没 without 了.

examples.r: Wǒ hē le liǎng bēi kāfēi.

tr.en: I drank two cups of coffee.

summary.en: 的 links a describer to a noun: 我的书 "my book", 红色的车 "the red car".

en: Whatever comes before 的 describes whatever comes after it, like English "'s" or "of".
With close relationships and very common pairs, 的 is often dropped: 我妈妈, 中国人.
A long describer still goes before the noun: 我昨天买的书 "the book I bought yesterday".

title.en: Question words: 什么, 谁, 哪儿, 几, 怎么

summary.en: Put the question word where the answer would go: 你叫什么？ 我叫小明.

en: Chinese does not move question words to the front. Say the statement and replace the unknown part.
什么 "what", 谁 "who", 哪儿 / 哪里 "where", 几 "how many (small numbers)", 怎么 "how", 为什么 "why".
Do not add 吗 to these questions.

concepts.pattern: Statement with the unknown replaced by a question word

summary.en: Turn a statement into a yes/no question by adding 吗 at the end: 你是老师吗？

en: Word order stays exactly the same as the statement. Only 吗 is added at the end.
Answer by repeating the verb: 你忙吗？ 忙 / 不忙. Chinese has no single word for "yes".
Do not use 吗 together with a question word like 什么 or 谁.

summary.en: 吧 at the end makes a suggestion ("let's ...") or checks a guess ("..., right?"): 我们走吧.

en: 我们 + verb + 吧 is the everyday "let's ...".
Statement + 吧？ asks for confirmation of something you already think is true: 你是老师吧？
吧 is softer than an order: 你坐吧 "go ahead and sit".

examples.r: Nǐ shì xīn lái de ba?

summary.en: A 比 B + adjective means "A is more ... than B": 他比我高 "he is taller than me". Never add 很.

en: The adjective stays plain. 他比我很高 is a classic mistake.
To say "a lot more", add 多了 or 得多 after the adjective: 今天比昨天冷多了.
For "not as ... as", use 没有: 我没有他高.

tr.en: My older brother is older than me.
This one is cheaper than that one.

summary.en: 呢 after a noun asks "what about ...?": 我很好，你呢？ It also softens questions.

en: Noun + 呢 bounces the last question to someone or something else.
At the end of a question with a question word, 呢 makes it softer: 你在做什么呢？
呢 can also mark an ongoing action: 他在睡觉呢 "he is sleeping".

examples.r: Wǒ shì Měiguó rén, nǐ ne?

title.en: Measure words: 个, 本, 杯 and friends

summary.en: Between a number (or 这/那) and a noun you need a measure word: 三个人, 一本书, 两杯水.

en: Chinese cannot say "three people" directly. It says "three [unit] people": 三个人.
个 is the general measure word and works for people and many things. Others match the shape or type: 本 for books, 杯 for cups of drinks, 张 for flat things, 只 for many animals.
Use 两, not 二, before a measure word: 两个 "two".

concepts.pattern: Number / 这 / 那 + measure word + noun

examples.r: Qǐng gěi wǒ yì bēi shuǐ.

tr.en: Please give me a glass of water.

title.en: 想, 要, 会, 能: want, will, can

summary.en: 想 "would like", 要 "want / will", 会 "know how to", 能 "be able to". They go right before the main verb.

en: 想 is soft: 我想喝水 "I would like some water". 要 is firmer and can mean "going to".
会 is a learned skill: 我会说中文. 能 is ability or permission in a situation: 我今天不能去.
Negate with 不: 不想, 不会, 不能. Note that the negative of 要 is usually 不想.

concepts.pattern: Subject + 想 / 要 / 会 / 能 + verb

tr.en: I would like to go to China.

summary.en: 有 means "have" (我有一个哥哥) and, after a place, "there is" (桌子上有一本书).

en: Person + 有 + thing is possession.
Place + 有 + thing means "there is / there are". Put the place first.
有 is negated with 没, never 不: 没有.

tr.en: There are a lot of people here.

title.en: 在 (zài): where something is or happens

summary.en: 在 + place says where: 我在家 "I am at home", 他在学校学习 "he studies at school".

en: As a verb, 在 means "to be located at": 书在桌子上.
Before another verb, 在 + place says where the action happens. The place comes before the action, unlike English.
Negate with 不: 他不在家 "he is not home".

summary.en: Use 是 to link two nouns: 我是学生 "I am a student". Do not use it before adjectives.

en: 是 links a subject to a noun or noun phrase, like English "am / is / are". It never changes form: 我是, 你是, 他们是.
Before an adjective, Chinese uses 很 instead of 是 (see the 很 + adjective concept). 我是高 is wrong; say 我很高.
To negate, put 不 in front: 我不是老师 "I am not a teacher".

summary.en: 也 "also" and 都 "all / both" go after the subject and before the verb: 我也去, 我们都去.

en: Both words are adverbs. They always sit before the verb, never at the end of the sentence.
都 points back to a plural subject: 他们都是学生 "they are all students".
When used together, the order is 也都: 我们也都喜欢.

title.en: 没 / 没有 (méi yǒu): "did not" and "do not have"

summary.en: 没有 means "do not have". 没 before a verb means it did not happen: 我没去 "I did not go".

en: 有 "to have" is always negated with 没, never 不: 我没有钱 "I have no money".
Before an action verb, 没 or 没有 says the action did not happen (or has not happened yet): 他还没来 "he has not come yet".
Do not add 了 after a verb negated with 没.

concepts.pattern: Subject + 没(有) + verb / 没有 + noun

tr.en: He did not go to work yesterday.

summary.en: 不 negates the present, the future, habits and wishes: 我不喝咖啡 "I do not drink coffee".

en: Put 不 directly before the verb or adjective you want to negate.
不 is for things in general, now or later, and for what you want or will do. For things that did not happen, use 没 instead.
不 changes to bú before a fourth tone: 不是 bú shì, 不对 bú duì.

summary.en: Adjectives work like verbs in Chinese. Put 很 before them: 她很忙 "she is busy". No 是 needed.

en: In Chinese an adjective can be the whole predicate. You do not need a word for "is".
A bare adjective sounds like a comparison (他高 "he is the taller one"), so speakers add 很 as a neutral link. Here 很 often does not mean "very".
Negate with 不 and drop 很: 天气不好 "the weather is not good".
